title: Data Engineering 2
summary: The second-year sequel, moving from building a pipeline to running one that survives contact with production.

syllabus.title: Synchronous & Asynchronous Data Flows
points: The two flow models set side by side, and the different failure modes each one hands the engineer downstream.
Choosing between them from the coupling and latency a system can actually tolerate.

Lab: the same ingestion written twice, once as a blocking request-response call and once decoupled behind a queue, then stalled on purpose to see which one loses records and which one only loses time.

syllabus.title: Resilient Pipeline Design
points: Retry management and recovery paths, designed on the assumption that failure is the normal case rather than the exception.
Orchestration, scheduling and backfills with Apache Airflow.
Lab: a multi-task Airflow DAG authored with task-level retries, exponential backoff and idempotent writes, then made to fail mid-run and repaired with a dated backfill over the missing window.

syllabus.title: Processing at Volume
points: Distributed processing with Apache Spark over PostgreSQL sources.
Lab: a join-and-aggregate transformation written in Spark against tables read from PostgreSQL, then reworked once the query plan showed where the shuffle was, and the two runs compared.

syllabus.title: Logging & Monitoring
points: Structured logging and error tracking with Loguru.
Monitoring, dashboards and alerting in Datadog.
Lab: the pipeline instrumented with structured Loguru records carrying run and task identifiers, shipped into a Datadog dashboard, with an alert wired to the failure rate and proved by triggering it.

syllabus.title: Packaging & Delivery
points: Pipelines containerised with Docker; datasets and models versioned with DVC.
Automated build and publish through GitHub Actions into the GitHub Container Registry.

Lab: a pipeline packaged into a Docker image with its dataset placed under DVC, and a GitHub Actions workflow that builds, tags and pushes to the GitHub Container Registry on every commit to the main branch.

capstone.title: Fault-Tolerant Ingestion Pipeline
points: The four-hour project session: one pipeline carrying data from a PostgreSQL source through a Spark transformation into an analytical target, scheduled as an Airflow DAG with retries and a working backfill path.
Operability was graded alongside the data flow: structured Loguru logging surfaced on a Datadog dashboard, the whole pipeline containerised with Docker, and the input dataset reproducible from DVC.
Delivered as a repository that runs from a single command, with an architecture diagram and a short written defence of where each retry, timeout and alert threshold was set, and why.

title: Data Engineering 1
summary: The first-year data engineering course: how analytical data is stored, moved, and processed at a volume that no longer fits one machine.

syllabus.title: Big Data Fundamentals
points: What changes once data outgrows a single machine, and why that reshapes the tooling around it.
Lab: the same aggregation run over a dataset held whole in memory and then over one read and partitioned in chunks, timed on both, to find the point where the single-machine habit stops working.

syllabus.title: Data Warehousing
points: Why analytical storage is shaped differently from the transactional systems it draws from.
Warehouse modelling worked against PostgreSQL.

Lab: a star schema designed from a normalised operational source (one fact table, conformed dimensions, explicit grain) and created in PostgreSQL, then queried to show what the denormalisation bought.

syllabus.title: ETL Architectures
points: Extract, transform and load followed from source system through to warehouse.
Transformations written in Python.

Lab: a Python ETL job extracting from the operational database, cleaning and conforming the records, and loading them into the star schema from the previous lab so the job can be re-run without duplicating rows.

syllabus.title: Processing at Volume
points: Distributed data processing with Apache Spark.

Lab: the same transformation rewritten as Spark DataFrame operations and run against a larger extract, set beside the single-machine Python version to see where the distributed one starts paying for itself.

syllabus.title: Analytics & Reporting
points: Closing the loop: warehouse data out into a Power BI report.
Lab: Power BI connected to the warehouse and a report built over the star schema, with the measures defined in the model rather than hard-coded into each visual.

capstone.title: Source-to-Dashboard Warehouse
points: The four-hour project session: the whole path in one piece, from a raw operational source to a published Power BI dashboard, built on the schema each team had modelled themselves.
Extraction and loading in Python, the heavier transformation step in Apache Spark, and the modelled tables served from PostgreSQL.
Delivered as the schema definition, the ETL code and the report, and defended on the modelling decisions (grain, keys, what was left out) rather than on the appearance of the dashboard.

title: Machine Learning
summary: The programme’s applied machine learning course, taken from stating a deterministic domain problem as a learnable one to deciding whether the result means anything or the experiment has to be redesigned.

syllabus.title: Supervised Learning
points: The frame, and what makes it hard. The ULB card fraud frame: 284,807 labelled card transactions, 492 of them fraud, so the only class worth predicting is 0.17% of the rows.

The accuracy trap. A model that never predicts fraud is already 99.83% accurate on that frame, so accuracy is never read on its own here: it is reported beside F1, and the gap between the two is the thing the module teaches students to look at.

The data problems worth checking for. Nulls, duplicates and class balance, run as a first pass before anything is fitted. On this frame nothing is missing and nothing is dirty, which is the useful result: the imbalance is the only real defect, and it is where the remaining effort goes.

Feature engineering under constraint. 28 of the 30 columns are anonymised principal components with no domain meaning attached, so Time and Amount are the only two columns a new feature can be built from. The limit is the exercise.

Scaling, and the split that comes before it. Normalisation with Scikit-learn and a stratified train/test split, so that 492 positives cannot land unevenly across the two halves, with the point that scaling decides whether the logistic regression converges and does nothing at all for a tree.

Which tabular model, and where each one stops. Decision trees, random forests and logistic regression set against what each of them assumes about the data, argued from a Matplotlib look at the frame rather than picked by reputation, and including the models that are the wrong tool for a problem this shape.

The parameters that decide a fit, sorted by what owns them. Batch size, epochs and convergence tolerance belong to anything fitted iteratively; depth, minimum leaf size and number of estimators belong to the tree family. Knowing which knob exists on which model is half of what tuning is.

Lab: twelve students in three teams of four, one estimator per team (decision tree, random forest, logistic regression) fitted in Scikit-learn over a single shared Pandas preparation in Google Colab, then scored on the same accuracy and F1 so that the three sets of results are numbers which can actually be compared across the room.

homework.title: Fraud Detection Benchmark
points: Individual, in Google Colab, and deliberately the inverse of the lab: the dataset and the two metrics are fixed, and every student is free on all three of the levers that decide a score.
The three levers: which features are selected and how they are prepared, which estimator is fitted, and what parameters it is fitted with.
Submitted as a commented notebook carrying the best accuracy and F1 the student reached, with the run that produced those two numbers reproducible from the notebook itself.
The comments are the argument: which of the three levers moved the score, by how much, and which one turned out not to matter.

syllabus.title: Gradient Descent & Optimisation
points: Gradient descent taught as the mechanism underneath model fitting rather than as a library call.
The parameters that decide whether it converges at all.
Lab: gradient descent implemented from the derivative upward in NumPy, with the loss traced across learning rates until it stalled at one end and diverged at the other.

syllabus.title: Unsupervised Learning & Clustering
points: Finding structure without labels, and where that is the honest framing of a problem.
K-Means end to end: assignment, centroid update, and the choice of k.
Lab: K-Means written by hand (assignment step, centroid update, convergence test) checked against the Scikit-learn implementation, with k argued from inertia and silhouette rather than picked.

syllabus.title: Model Evaluation
points: The techniques that separate a model fitting its training data from one that generalises.
Results inspected as Matplotlib plots, not only as a single score.

Lab: a classifier cross-validated and then read properly: confusion matrix, precision and recall against a deliberately imbalanced target, and a Matplotlib learning curve used to tell underfitting from overfitting.

syllabus.title: The Practical Workflow
points: The whole path in one piece: data pulled from PostgreSQL, prepared in Pandas, fitted in Scikit-learn, evaluated and plotted.

Lab: that path written as one reproducible script (query, preparation, fitted pipeline, evaluation) with the model and its metrics persisted together so a result can be traced back to the run that produced it.

capstone.title: Applied Prediction Study
points: The four-hour project session: a supervised problem carried from a PostgreSQL extract to a defended conclusion, with the model choice argued from the evaluation rather than asserted.
A Scikit-learn pipeline over Pandas preparation, tuned by cross-validated search and measured against a trivial baseline that had to be beaten for the result to count.
Delivered as a notebook with the Matplotlib figures the claims rest on, and graded on whether the evaluation actually supports what the report concludes.
